article_title: Real Progress in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation
citation: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2014). Real progress in Maryland: Student learning objectives and teacher and principal evaluation. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. http://marylandpublicschools.org/MSDE/programs/tpe/index.html
title: In SLO implementation, the process of thinking through the inter-related components matters most
description: Drawing on fifteen years of SLO practice and research, the report holds that the value of Student Learning Objectives lies in the deliberative process rather than the compliance artifact: "The process of thinking through the inter-related components of the SLO and their implications for instruction is what matters most." The SLO process should foster planning and delivery of instruction through data use and systematic analysis, and motivate performance through growth targets set by both teachers and students. Districts must balance manageability with rigor and standardization with customization, and would benefit from state guidance on how much flexibility schools may use while preserving comparability and trust.
requirements: Districts must strike a thoughtful balance between manageability and a thorough, rigorous process, and between standardization and customization
constraints: The report presents this as a national lesson from fifteen years of SLO practice and research rather than a finding tested within this study's own data
target_learners: K-12 teachers and principals developing and implementing SLOs
target_learning_goals: Instructional planning and delivery informed by data, and student growth through teacher- and student-set targets
examples: The report cites a teacher who examined baseline data, found an initial goal less lofty than thought, and reset it to be an attainable but more challenging goal
key_sources: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2014). Real progress in Maryland: Student learning objectives and teacher and principal evaluation. WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center. http://marylandpublicschools.org/MSDE/programs/tpe/index.html

article_title: Change in Practice in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation
citation: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2015). Change in Practice in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation. Mid-Atlantic Comprehensive Center (WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center).
title: Student Learning Objectives (SLOs) as an evidence-based instructional process
description: The report frames SLOs as “an evidence-based instructional process for improving educator effectiveness and student achievement,” and the predominant measure of student growth for teachers and principals within Maryland's TPE system. State models allot 30%-50% of the total evaluation rating to SLOs, with no single SLO counting for more than 35% of the total performance score. The Maryland Teacher and Principal Evaluation Guidebook, Version 3 emphasizes using SLOs as an ongoing, iterative, and collaborative process spanning data review, SLO development, conferences, and integration of results.
requirements: Districts must establish processes for setting, reviewing, assessing, and aligning SLOs, provide SLO training per state guidelines, and document a verification process to validate consistency, comparability, quality and rigor of SLOs and evaluation results
constraints: No single SLO may count for more than 35% of the total performance score
SLO weighting in overall ratings varies by district under local control
target_learning_goals: setting measurable growth targets for student learning
selecting learning content and research-based instructional strategies
examples: MSDE provided tools including SLO templates, guiding questions, a quality rating rubric, and crosswalks between SLOs and observations and College and Career-Ready Standards
key_sources: Slotnik, W. J., Bugler, D., & Liang, G. (2015). Change in Practice in Maryland: Student Learning Objectives and Teacher and Principal Evaluation. Mid-Atlantic Comprehensive Center (WestEd and Community Training and Assistance Center). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED568386

article_title: Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features
citation: Rajesh Kumar, Nabeel Siddiqui, Alexander Fuchsberger. (2026). Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26687
title: Sliding-window stylometric detection protocol with disjoint user splits and median aggregation
description: A detection framework in which each document is split into "a pre-specified length of250 words and a stride of125words" windows, nine stylometric features are computed per window, and window-level probabilities are aggregated using a median rule with a 0.50 threshold for document-level classification. Disjoint sets of users are used for training and testing to prevent author-specific style leakage. The protocol was evaluated with eight classifiers on the IIITD-BU (Paraphrased) dataset of 180 samples from 90 participants.
requirements: Requires all windows from a given participant to be kept within the same training, validation, or test set to prevent data leakage
constraints: GPT-assisted in this dataset means responses written by paraphrasing GPT-generated content, not the broader range of AI-assistance practices
target_learning_goals: detecting GPT-assisted academic writing for academic integrity review
examples: The 90 participants were partitioned into 72 training participants (144 samples) and 18 held-out participants (36 samples), producing 722 windows in total
key_sources: Rajesh Kumar, Nabeel Siddiqui, Alexander Fuchsberger. (2026). Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26687

article_title: Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation
citation: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428
title: slidesqaqa: a Flask-based system for generating pedagogical questions from PDF slide decks
description: slidesqaqa is a single-server Python Flask application that takes a PDF presentation as input, renders each slide into a visual thumbnail, extracts native text with PyMuPDF, and coordinates a four-phase LLM workflow. The system outputs "a comprehensive, hierarchical JSON structure that details the deck's topics, categorizes slide roles, defines specific learning goals, and provides bounded, context-aware comprehension questions." A frontend UI serves as a real-time log viewer and data visualizer.
requirements: Requires PyMuPDF for document extraction and integration with the Google GenAI SDK for multimodal inference
constraints: Reliance on a specific proprietary LLM (Gemini) poses reproducibility and long-term stability risks if API models are updated or deprecated
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in technical lecture courses
target_learning_goals: comprehension of slide-based lecture content in technical subjects such as NLP and deep learning
examples: Evaluated on the "Self-Attention and Transformers" (cs224n-2024-lecture08-transformers) and "Neural Constituency Parsing" (cs288-sp23-neural-parsing) lecture decks
key_sources: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428

article_title: Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation
citation: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428
title: Structured JSON annotation schema with deck-level goals, slide roles, questions, and evaluation scores
description: The final output is "a structured JSON annotation containing deck-level goals, section structure, slide-level summaries, question sets, and evaluation scores." Each slide record carries modality type, role in deck, eligibility for questions, question budget, and question mix; each question carries a prompt, options, a bounded evidence-grounded answer, an evidence span, difficulty, purpose, and a 1-5 fidelity score. Reconciliation records include revised slide actions, uncovered learning goals, and redundancy warnings.
requirements: All outputs must conform to strongly typed JSON schemas enforced via Pydantic models
constraints: Coverage and scaffolding scores are null when a slide intentionally has no questions
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in technical lecture courses
target_learning_goals: machine-readable pedagogical annotation of lecture slides for question generation and quality assurance
examples: Appendix A prints the full schema, and Appendix B prints the exact system prompt strings for all four pipeline phases
key_sources: Salsman, J. (2026). Slide Deck Q&A Quality Assurance App: A Multi-Stage Pipeline for Pedagogical Question Generation. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26428

article_title: A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities
citation: Haft Stephanie L., Greiner de Magalhães Caroline, Hoeft Fumiko. (2023). A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/00222194221087383
title: Framework distinguishing SLD stigma (including stigma consciousness and self-stigma) from stereotype threat as two contributors to poorer outcomes in SLDs
description: The review organizes the literature around two related constructs: stigma, "the devaluation of an attribute based on negative attitudes, stereotypes, or beliefs," and stereotype threat, "a more specific situation in which an individual fears confirming those negative beliefs." Within stigma it distinguishes stigma consciousness (perception of societal views, e.g., worry over judgment and expected differential treatment) from self-stigma (internalization of those views). The SLD label can function as a stigmatizing marker, and the framework maps proximal mechanisms (e.g., anxiety, self-efficacy) onto downstream consequences (Figure 3).
requirements: Studies must measure SLD-specific stigma (stigma consciousness or internalized stigma) or experimentally induce stereotype threat in samples of individuals with SLDs
constraints: The review notes stereotype threat effects vary by sample, setting, outcome measure, and the type of threat-activating cue (blatant vs. indirect and subtle)
target_learners: children, adolescents, and adults with specific learning disabilities
examples: The review's Figure 3 summarizes connections between SLD-related stigma/stereotype threat, proximal mechanisms, downstream consequences, and moderating environmental and individual variables
key_sources: Haft Stephanie L., Greiner de Magalhães Caroline, Hoeft Fumiko. (2023). A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/00222194221087383

article_title: Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning Among School-Age Children
citation: Taveras Elsie M. MD, MPH; Rifas-Shiman Sheryl L. MPH; Bub Kristen L. EdD; Gillman Matthew W. MD, SM; Oken Emily MD, MPH. (2017). Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning among School-Age Children. Academic Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5545152/
title: Sleep duration as an early-life influence on child neurobehavioral processes (executive function, behavior, social-emotional functioning)
description: This framework holds that sleep duration across infancy and early childhood is prospectively associated with neurobehavioral processes in mid-childhood, measured via the BRIEF (executive function, including behavioral regulation and metacognition) and the SDQ (behavioral and social-emotional difficulties). The article frames sleep as "influencing neurobehavioral processes including executive function, behavior, or social-emotional functioning," and hypothesized that "insufficient sleep at multiple time points throughout childhood would be associated with poorer child executive function, behavior, and social-emotional functioning as independently reported by mothers and teachers." Findings support the framework for preschool and early school ages but not consistently for infancy.
requirements: Multi-rater assessment (mothers and teachers independently) across home and school settings to detect situation-specific difficulties
Longitudinal sleep data from infancy onward, with later models adjusted for sleep at earlier ages
Validated instruments: the 86-item BRIEF and 25-item SDQ
constraints: Associations were inconsistent for infancy; no lasting effect of the shortest infant sleep durations was found
Only sleep duration was examined as the exposure; sleep fragmentation, variability, and timing were not measured
Neurobehavioral functioning was measured only at age 7, limiting causal ordering inference
examples: Project Viva categorized sleep at three age periods against National Sleep Foundation recommendations and modeled associations with age-7 BRIEF and SDQ outcomes from mothers and teachers
key_sources: Taveras Elsie M. MD, MPH; Rifas-Shiman Sheryl L. MPH; Bub Kristen L. EdD; Gillman Matthew W. MD, SM; Oken Emily MD, MPH. (2017). Prospective Study of Insufficient Sleep and Neurobehavioral Functioning among School-Age Children. Academic Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5545152/

article_title: Perceived Neighborhood Safety and Adolescent School Functioning
citation: Martin-Storey, A., & Crosnoe, R. (2014). Perceived Neighborhood Safety and Adolescent School Functioning. Applied Developmental Science, 18(2), 61-75. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888691.2014.876276
title: Sliding-scale conceptual model linking neighborhood safety to school outcomes by formality of schooling processes
description: The article proposes a conceptual model in which the strength of the association between perceived neighborhood safety and a school outcome depends on how tied that outcome is to formal versus informal schooling processes. The authors "posited a 'sliding scale' of predictive power based on how much these school outcomes are tied to formal or informal processes of schooling": school attachment, tied to informal processes, should be most strongly associated with perceived safety; standardized test scores, tied to formal processes, least; and grades, which mix the two, fall in the middle. The study's findings partially supported this ordering.
requirements: Outcomes must be classifiable along a formal-to-informal continuum of schooling processes
constraints: The model was tested with correlational SECCYD data on 15-year-olds and only partially supported; causal directionality could not be ascertained
examples: The study compared test scores, GPA, and school attachment in one SEM framework and found attachment, the most socioemotional outcome, was the only one associated with perceived safety after controls.
key_sources: Martin-Storey, A., & Crosnoe, R. (2014). Perceived Neighborhood Safety and Adolescent School Functioning. Applied Developmental Science, 18(2), 61-75. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888691.2014.876276

article_title: Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature
citation: Oliveira, T., Nada, C., & Magalhães, A. (2024). Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231226336
title: Systematic literature review corpus of 54 documents on academic careers from 21 national contexts (Scopus and Scielo, 2000–2021)
description: The review's evidence base is a corpus of 54 selected documents assembled from searches of Scopus (475 results) and Scielo (39 results) in February 2022, screened in two levels from an initial pool of 509 entries after duplicate removal. The corpus "included both theoretical contributions and empirical findings from 21 different national contexts," published between 2000 and 2021 in English or Portuguese. Most documents came from English-primary-language countries (n = 33), and most employed qualitative designs, with interviews the largest data-collection technique (n = 24).
requirements: Access to Scopus and Scielo databases and the review's Boolean search string on academic careers
constraints: No article from Scielo remained after applying the selection criteria, and the corpus was overrepresented by research from English-primary-language countries
target_learners: Researchers studying academic careers and higher education work
target_learning_goals: Mapping the international literature on academic careers under marketization
examples: Searches in February 2022 yielded 475 Scopus and 39 Scielo entries; after screening, 54 documents were thematically analyzed.
key_sources: Oliveira, T., Nada, C., & Magalhães, A. (2024). Navigating an Academic Career in Marketized Universities: Mapping the International Literature. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543231226336

article_title: Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation.
citation: Paul Knuth and W. C. B., abstractors. (1910). Journal of Educational Psychology abstracts page: theory of sleep; T. H. Morgan, Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation. Science, 33: 789.
title: Theory of sleep as an actively induced passive state explained by cell energy and stimulus exhaustion
description: The abstracted theory explains sleep in terms of cell energy and stimulus exhaustion: living tissue discharges energy in response to a stimulus, and responsiveness has a limit, so that repeated stimulation of constant intensity eventually fails to incite a response. The abstract states that "the monotony of stimula- tion raises the threshold," and that an organism is asleep to an environment it fails to respond to while remaining awake to stimuli not yet exhausted. Sleep is characterized as an "actively induced passive state in relation to the external environment," developed out of the hypnoidal state, with implications for dream-life and subconscious activities.
requirements: The account presupposes that responsiveness of living tissue to a stimulus has a finite limit, so that constant-intensity stimulation progressively loses effectiveness.
constraints: The theory is stated at the level of cells and organisms generally, not derived from learning tasks or instructional settings.
target_learners: human organisms generally, as discussed in the source
target_learning_goals: understanding responsiveness and threshold changes under repeated stimulation
examples: The abstract describes subjects passing into and out of sleep through a brief, unstable hypnoidal state oscillating between waking and sleep or hypnosis.
key_sources: Paul Knuth and W. C. B., abstractors. (1910). Journal of Educational Psychology abstracts page: theory of sleep; T. H. Morgan, Chance or Purpose in the Origin and Evolution of Adaptation. Science, 33: 789. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0065426

article_title: Light on some aspects of education in England.
citation: L. Z. (1920). New Publications. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Classified bibliography of pertinent educational literature in Sleight's volume
description: The reviewed book closes with reference apparatus the reviewer explicitly notes: "The book contains a classified bibliography of pertinent educational literature." This bibliography supports readers, particularly students of comparative education, in following up the organizational and curricular topics treated across the volume's chapters, from school organization and buildings to teacher training and the Education Act of 1918.
requirements: Must stay pertinent to the educational topics of the volume and be classified for use
target_learning_goals: understanding English school organization and curricula

article_title: How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain
citation: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y
title: SLIMM framework: mPFC detects schema resonance and integrates new information while inhibiting the hippocampus
description: The SLIMM framework is a systems-level neuroscientific model of schema-mediated memory cited and described in this review. It holds that "the mPFC detects resonance from an activated schema and then acts to directly integrate newly learned information", a process usually achieved through offline processes such as (re)consolidation. The review notes the hippocampus is not related to integrating new information with existing schemas in this framework and "it is suggested to be inhibited by the mPFC" in such situations.
requirements: Applies to human, whole-brain, systems-level accounts of schema storage, access and update involving the hippocampus and mPFC
constraints: The review states specifics of consolidation processes are still up to debate, and the framework's claims are posed as proposals rather than tested conclusions
key_sources: van Kesteren, M. T. R. & Meeter, M. (2020). How to optimize knowledge construction in the brain. npj Science of Learning 5:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0064-y

article_title: Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation
citation: Charlène Truong, Célia Ruffino, Jérémie Gaveau, Olivier White, Pauline M. Hilt and Charalambos Papaxanthis. (2023). Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00176-9
title: Sleep-proximity account of motor consolidation: sleep shortly after training protects the new motor memory from interference and forgetting
description: The article proposes that consolidation of a newly trained motor skill depends on the temporal proximity between training and sleep rather than on time of day per se. Training close to a night of sleep enables offline learning, while a full waking day between training and sleep exposes the labile memory to retroactive interference and forgetting. The authors state that "a training session close to sleep could protect against memory deterioration induced by additional memories (retroactive interferences)" and that "the morning group, spending more time awake than the afternoon and evening groups, could be more exposed to interferences". Alternative explanations are acknowledged but not resolved.
requirements: Training that ends close enough to sleep for the night of sleep to occur soon after acquisition
constraints: The authors state it remains to be determined whether it is the time of day or the proximity between training and sleep that influences consolidation, suggesting nap designs as a test
Sleep stages were not quantified in the study; only the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index was used
target_learners: Adults practicing fine motor skills, including sports and rehabilitation populations
target_learning_goals: Long-term retention and offline consolidation of newly acquired motor skills
examples: G8sleep retested 2 h after waking matched G8pm's offline gain, while G8awake retested before sleep showed none
key_sources: Charlène Truong, Célia Ruffino, Jérémie Gaveau, Olivier White, Pauline M. Hilt and Charalambos Papaxanthis. (2023). Time of day and sleep effects on motor acquisition and consolidation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00176-9

article_title: Action video games normalise the phonemic awareness in pre-readers at risk for developmental dyslexia
citation: Bertoni, S., Andreola, C., Mascheretti, S., Franceschini, S., Ruffino, M., Trezzi, V., Molteni, M., Sali, M. E., Salandi, A., Gaggi, O., Palazzi, C., Gori, S. & Facoetti, A. (2024). Action video games normalise the phonemic awareness in pre-readers at risk for developmental dyslexia. npj Science of Learning 9, 25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00230-0
title: Sluggish attentional shifting as slow multisensory accumulation of evidence: the AVG mechanism account
description: The article frames phonological deficits in dyslexia as arising from a sluggish attentional shifting equivalent to a slow "accumulation of multisensory evidence". AVGs, with high-speed, spatiotemporally unpredictable stimuli and strong reward signals, are hypothesised to accelerate evidence accumulation and place the brain in a more plastic state, thereby improving phonemic discrimination in at-risk pre-readers. The account links right-lateralised attentional networks (alerting, ventral stimulus-driven control, the "When" pathway, salience network) to phonemic awareness development.
requirements: Training targeting stimulus-driven and goal-directed attentional control with reward signals, as AVGs provide
constraints: The neural account is a hypothesis; the study collected no neural-correlate data, and the authors state future studies are needed to test this neurobiological hypothesis
target_learners: Pre-readers (kindergarten) at risk for developmental dyslexia
examples: At-risk pre-readers played the commercial action game Space Invaders Extreme 2 for at least 20 sessions of 45 min over 1.5 months
key_sources: Bertoni, S., Andreola, C., Mascheretti, S., Franceschini, S., Ruffino, M., Trezzi, V., Molteni, M., Sali, M. E., Salandi, A., Gaggi, O., Palazzi, C., Gori, S. & Facoetti, A. (2024). Action video games normalise the phonemic awareness in pre-readers at risk for developmental dyslexia. npj Science of Learning 9, 25. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00230-0

article_title: The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction
citation: Ping Li and Hyeonjeong Jeong. (2020). The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction. npj Science of Learning 5:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0068-7
title: SL2 neural network: a right-heavy IPL–IFG–CN loop plus visual cortex for social L2 learning
description: The article proposes a brain network underlying social L2 learning comprising the inferior parietal regions (SMG, AG), IFG, caudate nucleus, and visual regions (LG). It stresses that "this network highlights the stronger role of the right-hemisphere brain regions as compared with the typical left-lateralized language networks", with IFG handling lexical-semantic processing bilaterally and the right-hemisphere cortical and subcortical regions participating in social learning. The authors hypothesize this network dynamically connects to mPFC and TPJ of the theory-of-mind network.
requirements: Understanding how the areas collaborate during learning and memory requires a network-science analysis of functional/structural brain patterns
constraints: The hypothesized dynamic connection to the ToM network "needs to be examined carefully by comparing learning with social interaction versus without"; how the left frontal IFG and right parietal IPL form a dynamic network "remains to be understood"
target_learning_goals: neurocognitive mechanisms of socially grounded L2 vocabulary learning
key_sources: Ping Li and Hyeonjeong Jeong. (2020). The social brain of language: grounding second language learning in social interaction. npj Science of Learning 5:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-0068-7

article_title:
Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple 
memory systems
citation: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2
title: Slow/fast mode framework of oscillatory dynamics across memory systems
description: The review organizes oscillatory dynamics in the hippocampus, cortex, and striatum into two brain states: a slow mode during quiet rest or SWS, characterized by hippocampal large irregular activity plus cortical and striatal delta, and a fast mode during active waking and REM, typified by theta in the hippocampus and its targets and gamma in the rest of cortex. It proposes that "The fast mode is associated with the ef ﬁcacious encoding and retrieval of both declarative and procedural memories" while the slow mode regulates offline declarative consolidation. The framework explains why different memory types depend on different sleep stages.
requirements: Shared low-level circuit constraints across hippocampal, cortical, and striatal networks that generate comparable delta, theta, and gamma rhythms
constraints: The review notes most supporting evidence is correlational and REM consolidation physiology is less well understood than SWS consolidation
target_learners: adults and animals forming declarative and procedural memories
target_learning_goals: memory consolidation across declarative and procedural systems
examples: The review maps SWS delta and SWR reactivation onto declarative consolidation and REM hippocampal-amygdala theta onto emotional memory consolidation
key_sources: Drew B. Headley and Denis Paré. (2017). Common oscillatory mechanisms across multiple memory systems. npj Science of Learning 2:1. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-016-0001-2

article_title: An appraisal of the effectiveness of selected instructional sound motion pictures and silent filmstrips in elementary school instruction
citation: Slattery, Sister M. Jamesetta. (1953). An Appraisal of the Effectiveness of Selected Instructional Sound Motion Pictures and Silent Filmstrips in Elementary School Instruction. The Catholic University of America Press. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED073727
title: Rotation-design comparison of sound motion pictures and silent filmstrips in fifth-grade social studies
description: An experiment in which "The experimental population of 422 fifth-grade pupils from nine elementary schools of Rochester, New York, was set up in six divisions according to a rotation design." Divisions were equated on IQ, mental age, and initial test scores, and the rotation involved four sound motion pictures and four silent filmstrips, with participation consisting of reading verbal material aloud and answering script questions.
requirements: Divisions equated on IQ, mental age, and initial test scores
constraints: Scope limited to fifth-grade social studies in Rochester, New York elementary schools
target_learning_goals: Informational and conceptual learning in social studies
key_sources: Slattery, Sister M. Jamesetta. (1953). An Appraisal of the Effectiveness of Selected Instructional Sound Motion Pictures and Silent Filmstrips in Elementary School Instruction. The Catholic University of America Press. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED073727

article_title: A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities.
citation: Haft, S. L., Greiner de Magalhães, C., & Hoeft, F. (2023). A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/00222194221087383
title: Framework of SLD-related stigma and stereotype threat linking proximal mechanisms to downstream consequences
description: The review organizes its findings in a summary model (Figure 3) in which SLD-related stigma and stereotype threat connect to "factors that may be more proximal mechanisms" (middle box, e.g., internalized stigma, help-seeking, giving up behavior, maladaptive coping) and to "more downstream consequences" (bottom box, e.g., anxiety, depression, self-esteem, academic performance). Environmental and individual variables may influence the potency of stigma and stereotype threat. The framework draws on prior reviews (Pennington et al., 2016) and positions motivation-related variables as candidate mediators of stereotype threat effects on exam performance.
requirements: Longitudinal studies are needed to identify mechanisms by which external stigma influences mental health and to test mediating relationships
constraints: All 11 stigma–psychological-adjustment studies were cross-sectional, so mechanistic claims remain hypothesized
target_learners: individuals with specific learning disabilities across childhood, adolescence, and adulthood
examples: The review maps its 60 effect sizes onto proximal mechanisms (e.g., thought intrusion, academic self-efficacy) and downstream outcomes (e.g., self-esteem, academic performance) in its Figure 3 summary model.
key_sources: Haft, S. L., Greiner de Magalhães, C., & Hoeft, F. (2023). A Systematic Review of the Consequences of Stigma and Stereotype Threat for Individuals With Specific Learning Disabilities. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/00222194221087383

article_title: Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Fontaine G, Cossette S, Maheu-Cadotte M-A, Mailhot T, Deschênes M-F, Mathieu-Dupuis G, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Dubé V. (2019). Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025252
title: Three main adaptive e-learning platforms used in health professions education: SlideTutor, Smart Sparrow and PALM
description: The review identifies three main adaptive e-learning platforms across the 21 studies: "SlideTutor (n=4), Smart Sparrow (n=4) and the Perceptual Adaptive Learning Module (PALM, n=3)". SlideTutor is an AEE with algorithmic adaptivity providing dermopathology virtual-slide cases supervised by the system, using an expert knowledge base of evidence-diagnosis relationships to build a dynamic solution graph and determine the optimal instructional sequence. Smart Sparrow uses designed adaptivity, letting educators set adaptivity factors to specify how the system adapts the instructional sequence or provides feedback. PALM uses algorithmic adaptivity with adaptive response-time-based sequencing that dynamically spaces learning items based on each learner's accuracy and speed.
requirements: Educators or algorithms must specify adaptivity factors and the instructional sequence; PALM requires interactive learning trials generating accuracy and speed data
constraints: SlideTutor cases are specific to dermopathology virtual slides; Smart Sparrow custom learning paths "can be more or less personalised"
examples: Studies using these platforms trained learners in dermopathology, diagnostic cytopathology, diagnostic imaging, electrocardiography and fetal heart rate interpretation
key_sources: Fontaine G, Cossette S, Maheu-Cadotte M-A, Mailhot T, Deschênes M-F, Mathieu-Dupuis G, Côté J, Gagnon M-P, Dubé V. (2019). Efficacy of adaptive e-learning for health professionals and students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2018-025252

article_title: What Is the Minimum Information Needed to Estimate Average Treatment Effects in Education RCTs?
citation: Schochet, Peter Z. (2013). What is the Minimum Information Needed to Estimate Average Treatment Effects in Education RCTs? SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. http://www.whitehouse.gov/sites/default/files/omb/memoranda/2013/m-13-17.pdf
title: State longitudinal data systems (SLDSs) supported by the IES SLDS Grant Program
description: SLDSs are state administrative data systems containing statewide student data that can be linked over time and potentially to additional data sources. The abstract states: "Since 2006, 47 states have received at least one grant from IES' SLDS Grant Program to support the design, development, implementation, and expansion of the data systems." Their key advantage is typically including data from all public schools in a state, making them a candidate outcome-data source for opportunistic experiments.
requirements: Researcher access to the aggregate statistics needed for impact estimation, subject to state confidentiality rules
constraints: Access to identifiable records is often difficult due to state data confidentiality concerns
target_learning_goals: Measuring student achievement outcomes for intervention evaluations
examples: The paper's demonstration examples use outcome data of the kind held in SLDSs: math or reading test scores of elementary school students

article_title: Effects of Video-Based Cooperative, Competitive and Individualized Instructional Strategies on the Performance of Senior Secondary Schools Students in Geometry
citation: Gambari, A. I., Shittu, A. T., Daramola, F. O., & James, M. (2016). Effects Of Video-Based Cooperative, Competitive And Individualized Instructional Strategies On The Performance Of Senior Secondary Schools Students In Geometry. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Sciences, 4(4). https://www.moj-es.net
title: Slavin's four theoretical perspectives of cooperative learning
description: The article reviews Slavin's (1997) framework distinguishing four theoretical perspectives on why cooperative learning works: "motivational, social cohesion, developmental, and cognitive elaboration perspectives". The motivational perspective focuses on reward or goal structures under which students operate; the social cohesion perspective holds that students help group mates because they care about the group; the developmental perspective assumes interaction around appropriate tasks increases mastery of critical concepts; and the cognitive elaboration perspective stresses that elaboration prepares the individual for cognitive re-structure and rehearsal. The article uses this framework, alongside Deutsch's cooperative/competitive goal structures and constructivist learning theory, as its theoretical background for predicting cooperative video instruction advantages.
requirements: Cooperative learning depends on goal structures under which students operate, with reward structures creating positive interdependence among group members
examples: The study operationalized cooperation via three-member heterogeneous groups with assigned roles, consensus decisions, individual accountability tasks, and weekly recognition of high-scoring teams
key_sources: Gambari, A. I., Shittu, A. T., Daramola, F. O., & James, M. (2016). Effects Of Video-Based Cooperative, Competitive And Individualized Instructional Strategies On The Performance Of Senior Secondary Schools Students In Geometry. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Sciences, 4(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1116321

article_title: The Effect of Phonetic Transcription on Iranian EFL Students' Word Stress Learning
citation: Ghorbani, M. R. (2019). The effect of phonetic transcription on Iranian EFL students' word stress learning. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 15(2), 400-410. https://www.jlls.org
title: Speech Learning Model account: target-like perception of L2 sounds precedes and supports target-like production
description: The article frames its intervention with the Speech Learning Model (SLM), in which "the L2 perception is thought to be a prerequisite to production", and learners are more likely to discover phonological differences when L1-L2 sound differences are great. The study's findings are read as lending support to the SLM claim that target-like perception can lead to target-like production, positioning listening perception work as the route to improved spoken English in instructed contexts.
requirements: Perception training must precede or accompany production practice for the perception-to-production pathway to operate
constraints: The account is applied to adult learners in formal instructional settings; the article notes exposure alone will not do for adults
target_learning_goals: English lexical stress perception and production
examples: The study trained listening perception through transcription work and interpreted post-test gains as support for the SLM claim
key_sources: Ghorbani, M. R. (2019). The effect of phonetic transcription on Iranian EFL students' word stress learning. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 15(2), 400-410. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1220802

article_title: Learning L2 Pronunciation with a Mobile Speech Recognizer: French /y/
citation: Denis Liakin, Walcir Cardoso and Natallia Liakina. (2015). Learning L2 pronunciation with a mobile speech recognizer: French /y/. CALICO Journal 32.1. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.v32i1.25962
title: Speech Learning Model and Perceptual Assimilation Model: perceptually similar (assimilable) L2 segments are harder to acquire than dissimilar ones
description: The article invokes Flege's Speech Learning Model and Best's Perceptual Assimilation Model as accounts of how L1 phonotactic knowledge filters foreign speech sounds. Flege's SLM "postulates that phonetically similar L2 sounds are more likely to be perceived via the L1 than those that are dissimilar", with similar sounds subsumed under existing L1 categories, producing foreign accent. Both models predict that new L2 segments that are perceptually similar (assimilable) will be harder to acquire than dissimilar ones; the authors conjecture French /y/ patterns with the similar case for their learners' L1s.
requirements: The models apply to L2 speech perception and learning where L1 phonological categories filter new L2 segments.
constraints: The article states it is premature and beyond the study's scope to determine definitively whether French /y/ patterns with the similar or dissimilar scenario for the L1s included.
target_learners: Adult L2 French learners at elementary (A2) proficiency
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of the French vowel /y/ in production and perception
examples: The authors conjecture that English, Farsi and Spanish speakers' /u/ and Portuguese speakers' /i/ make /y/ assimilable, explaining its documented difficulty.
key_sources: Denis Liakin, Walcir Cardoso and Natallia Liakina. (2015). Learning L2 pronunciation with a mobile speech recognizer: French /y/. CALICO Journal 32.1. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.v32i1.25962

article_title: Preliminary Findings from an Efficacy Study of a Distributed Leadership Model of School Organization
citation: Borman, K., Murphy, S. P., LoSasso, J., & Schlanger, L. (2013). Preliminary Findings from an Efficacy Study of a Distributed Leadership Model of School Organization. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract.
title: Systems Leadership for Middle Schools (SLMS) intervention: six Action Teams, a Guiding Coalition, and three support dimensions
description: SLMS is a whole-school intervention developed by Modern Red Schoolhouse that reorganizes a school's teachers and administrators onto six Action Teams, each headed by a teacher who also serves on the school's Guiding Coalition. Teams focus on family and community partnerships, curriculum and instruction, data analysis, technology, professional development, and school climate and culture, and are meant to replace standing and ad hoc committees. The program "is designed to provide support for middle school staff to effectively devise their own solutions to contextually specific problems" through three dimensions: structure, process, and technical knowledge, with MRSH facilitators providing on-site support during three-day visits.
requirements: MRSH facilitators provide on-site support, meeting separately with each of the six Action Teams and the Guiding Coalition, and with principals several times over three-day visits
constraints: Team membership is expected to reflect faculty makeup by department, grade level, experience, ethnicity, gender, and MBTI personality type
target_learning_goals: organizational capacity for school improvement, instructional coherence, and distributed leadership
examples: In the study, MRSH facilitators met with each of the six Action Teams and the Guiding Coalition at each treatment site during three-day visits
key_sources: Borman, K., Murphy, S. P., LoSasso, J., & Schlanger, L. (2013). Preliminary Findings from an Efficacy Study of a Distributed Leadership Model of School Organization. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED564091

article_title: Preservice Teachers Working with English Language Learners: A Meta-Synthesis of Service-Learning as an Effective Pedagogical Tool
citation: Toronyi, A. (2020). Preservice Teachers Working with English Language Learners: A Meta-Synthesis of Service-Learning as an Effective Pedagogical Tool. Journal of Service-Learning in Higher Education, 11. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022487107305259
title: Combine service-learning placements with methods courses that teach L2 theoretical foundations and structured reflection
description: This principle holds that SL placements for PSTs working with ELLs are effective pedagogical tools only when embedded in well-designed methods courses. As the author concludes, method courses must "address the theoretical foundations of L2 acquisition, provide well-orchestrated placements with the input of all stakeholders, and allow engaging and relevant class discussions reflecting on PSTs' experiences." Without this integration, deficit-model thinking may be reinforced rather than transformed.
requirements: Methods courses must address theoretical foundations of L2 acquisition
Placements must be well-orchestrated with input from all stakeholders
Class discussions must allow reflection on PSTs' SL experiences
constraints: Most studies did not go beyond 10-20 hours of SL within one semester
Daniel's (2014) refutational study found poorly prepared mentors reinforced deficit-model thinking
target_learning_goals: Preparing for culturally and linguistically diverse mainstream classrooms
Developing L2 methodologies and culturally relevant pedagogy
examples: Lund and Lee (2015) used a social-justice framework methods course enabling critical reflection that contributed to growing cultural humility among 10 PSTs in 10-week community placements
key_sources: Toronyi, A. (2020). Preservice Teachers Working with English Language Learners: A Meta-Synthesis of Service-Learning as an Effective Pedagogical Tool. Journal of Service-Learning in Higher Education, 11. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022487107305259

article_title: Group performance differences in reading, math, and science by fourth graders with and without communication disorders.
citation: Karasinski Courtney. (2026). Group performance differences in reading, math, and science by fourth graders with and without communication disorders. CoDAS. https://doi.org/10.1590/2317-1782/e20250322en
title: Speech-language pathologists should collaborate with content-area teachers to support academic success
description: The article concludes that collaborative practice between SLPs and content-area teachers is crucial for children with language impairment, given the role of language across the curriculum. It further recommends that SLPs partner with other professionals to support low-income children and that underperforming students be referred to SLPs for language screening. The author states "Collaborative practice between SLPs and content-area teachers is crucial for ensuring that children with language impairment achieve success in the classroom."
requirements: SLPs must find ways to partner with other professionals, including content-area teachers
examples: The article recommends referring children underperforming in academic subjects to SLPs for language ability screening.

article_title: Assessing Best Practices in a Simulated Lumbar Puncture Workshop With Medical Students.
citation: Dugan L, Rei KM, Ueno A, Mahutga J, Varma M. (2025). Assessing Best Practices in a Simulated Lumbar Puncture Workshop With Medical Students. The Permanente Journal. https://doi.org/10.7812/TPP/24.155
title: Simulated lumbar puncture workshop with validated binary checklist assessment for first-year medical students
description: A voluntary simulated lumbar puncture (sLP) workshop in which first-year medical students were taught via one of two methods and then performed a video-recorded sLP alone. Skill was scored with a modified validated procedural checklist with "internal consistency coefficient of 0.79 using Cronbach's α", simplified for first-year students, and video raters showed acceptable inter-rater reliability with "an intraclass correlation coefficient of 0.819". Each group received exactly 30 minutes of instruction and practice at a 2:1 student-to-facilitator ratio.
requirements: Facilitator fidelity confirmed via teaching method checklists (all facilitators achieved 100% fidelity in this study).
Video-recorded attempts scored by two raters using the binary checklist.
constraints: The checklist was simplified for first-year medical students (e.g., did not include writing a procedure note).
Students with any prior LP exposure through patient care or health care education were excluded.
target_learning_goals: acquiring the procedural skill of lumbar puncture in a simulated environment
examples: Thirty-five students participated; 41 attended the workshop from 130 invited, with 6 excluded for prior LP exposure.
key_sources: Dugan L, Rei KM, Ueno A, Mahutga J, Varma M. (2025). Assessing Best Practices in a Simulated Lumbar Puncture Workshop With Medical Students. The Permanente Journal. https://doi.org/10.7812/TPP/24.155

article_title: Improving Confidence in Performing Clinical Procedures Through Peer-Driven Training Sessions for Preclinical Medical Students.
citation: Bohrer Maxwell B. MD, Rodgers David L. EdD. (2025). Improving Confidence in Performing Clinical Procedures Through Peer-Driven Training Sessions for Preclinical Medical Students. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11542
title: Student-led procedure training session (SLPTS): four 30-minute simulation stations with presession videos, facilitator guides, and peer demonstrations
description: The SLPTS is an elective, evening, out-of-curriculum training session in which trained first- or second-year medical students facilitate four simulation stations: abscess incision and drainage, simple interrupted suturing, endotracheal intubation, and peripheral vein IV access. Each rotation included "a brief introduction to the procedure, including indications and contraindications to each procedure, a facilitator demonstration, and student practice time," with each station staffed by one or two instructors and eight learners. Author-owned presession videos and facilitator guides supported the stations.
requirements: Peer instructors attend a training session one week prior, with an emergency medicine physician present to ensure proper technique
Facilitator guides and presession videos prepared and expert-reviewed before implementation
Access to a simulation center with separate rooms and task trainers
constraints: Implemented electively outside the formal curriculum at a regional medical campus
Intubation station excluded medications, detailed indications and contraindications, and back-up airway options as beyond its scope
target_learning_goals: Confidence and introductory competence in basic suturing, abscess incision and drainage, endotracheal intubation, and peripheral vein access
examples: Seven peer instructors taught 37 learners in a 2-hour session at a simulation center, with an overhead camera used at the suturing station and a self-constructed video laryngoscope at the intubation station
key_sources: Bohrer Maxwell B. MD, Rodgers David L. EdD. (2025). Improving Confidence in Performing Clinical Procedures Through Peer-Driven Training Sessions for Preclinical Medical Students. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11542

article_title: Psychometric analysis of the Slovak version of the satisfaction with simulation experience scale (measurement invariance).
citation: Polónyiová K., Teličák P., Vitovič P., Hnilicová S. (2025). Psychometric analysis of the Slovak version of the satisfaction with simulation experience scale (measurement invariance). Medical Education Online, 30(1). https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2025.2534055
title: Slovak version of the Satisfaction with Simulation Experience (SSE) scale
description: An 18-item questionnaire rated on a 5-point Likert scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree, measuring "general student satisfaction with simulation experience and its three components: debriefing and reflection, clinical reasoning, and clinical learning." This study produced the first validated Slovak translation and the first administration of the SSE to medical students rather than nursing students. Raw data, R code and scale items are shared on OSF.
requirements: Forward and backward translation procedure with certified translators for new language versions
constraints: Validated in a single institution with a convenience sample of General Medicine students; convergent and discriminant validity not yet tested because no comparable Slovak-language instruments exist
target_learning_goals: assessing student satisfaction with simulation-based education
examples: Administered after three new simulation scenarios in Biophysics, Physiology, and Microbiology courses during winter semester 2024

article_title: Standardized learner simulation for debriefer training through video conference.
citation: Rhee Jiyoung, Park Hyun Soo. (2025). Standardized learner simulation for debriefer training through video conference. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.321
title: Standardized learner (SL) simulation debriefer training course delivered by video conference
description: A debriefer training course in which a trainer plays a standardized learner (an ICU nurse in a recorded 5-minute simulation-based healthcare education video) while each trainee practices debriefing, followed by immediate individual trainer feedback. Over 2 weeks there were "five training sessions of 100 minutes each," each targeting a different PEARLS framework element (reactions, descriptions, analysis, summary). Simulations were video recorded for OSAD rating and conducted on Zoom, with waiting trainees preparing and reflecting in a separate breakout room.
requirements: Trainers acting as SLs prepare scripted responses and response frames based on the PEARLS framework; trainees pre-watch the sample video and prepare a debriefing plan from provided self-learning materials (72 slides).
constraints: The course was structurally designed only for debriefing and could not train pre-briefing or facilitating; it used one SL and one sample video featuring one learner, and included a small number of participants.
target_learners: Novice physician debriefers who teach medical students or residents
target_learning_goals: Debriefing skills in simulation-based healthcare education and self-confidence in operating simulation classes
examples: Four beta tests preceded the course; the designers skipped pre-briefing and focused each session on one PEARLS element after the full format took over 2 hours, and moved individual feedback into separate Zoom breakout rooms.
key_sources: Rhee Jiyoung, Park Hyun Soo. (2025). Standardized learner simulation for debriefer training through video conference. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.321

article_title: "No pain, no gain": Simulation-based learning in teacher education: The mediating role of simulation hindrances.
citation: Levin, O., Frei-Landau, R., & Goldberg, C. (2025). "No pain, no gain": Simulation-based learning in teacher education: The mediating role of simulation hindrances. PLoS ONE, 20(1), e0317255. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317255
title: SLOTE scale: Simulation-based Learning Outcomes in Teacher Education questionnaire
description: The SLOTE scale is a validated 29-item questionnaire with 7-point Likert responses (not at all to very much) measuring the extent to which an SBL workshop produced specific outcomes. "Overall, this scale consists of three factors: peer reflective learning (α = .86), simulation-related hindrances (α = .74), and communication skills (α = .95)." It was developed and validated in the authors' previous study and used here to collect data from 370 workshop participants via a Google Form.
requirements: Administered after participation in an SBL workshop; developed and validated in the authors' prior study
constraints: Self-reported questionnaire, which the authors note may be subject to social desirability bias
examples: Used as the data-collection instrument for the SEM analysis in this study (N = 370, 2019–2020)
key_sources: Levin, O., Frei-Landau, R., & Goldberg, C. (2025). "No pain, no gain": Simulation-based learning in teacher education: The mediating role of simulation hindrances. PLoS ONE, 20(1), e0317255. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317255

article_title: The effect of spaced E-Learning on knowledge of basic life support and satisfaction of nursing students: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Ranjbar Fataneh, Sharif-Nia Hamid, Shiri Maryam, Rahmatpour Pardis. (2024). The effect of spaced E-Learning on knowledge of basic life support and satisfaction of nursing students: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05533-9
title: SLS-OLE instrument for student satisfaction with online learning environments
description: The Student Learning and Satisfaction in Online Learning Environments Instrument (SLS-OLE) is a 34-item questionnaire used in this study to measure nursing students' satisfaction with the online BLS course. It covers six domains — "course structure, learner interaction, student engagement, instructor presence, student satisfaction, perceived learning" — on a seven-point Likert scale. The researchers translated it into Persian, validated it with ten professors (CVI > 0.7, CVR > 0.62), and reported Cronbach's alpha values from 0.72 to 0.94 across domains.
requirements: Permission from the scale's developer, translation, and face and content validity evaluation by subject-matter professors before use in a new language or context
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in online courses
target_learning_goals: measuring satisfaction and perceived learning in online learning environments
examples: Both study groups completed the SLS-OLE after the BLS course; domain scores were compared between groups with t-tests.

article_title: The Impact of Systematic Laparoscopic Skills and Suture Training on Laparoscopic Hysterectomy Outcomes in a Brazilian Teaching Hospital.
citation: Lobão Gonçalves Anna Luiza, Ayroza-Ribeiro Helizabet Abdala, Lima Raquel Ferreira, Yonamine Aline Estefane Eras, Ohara Fabio, Ayroza-Ribeiro Paulo Augusto Galvão. (2019). The Impact of Systematic Laparoscopic Skills and Suture Training on Laparoscopic Hysterectomy Outcomes in a Brazilian Teaching Hospital. RBGO Gynecology & Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0039-1700587
title: Systematic Laparoscopic Skills and Suture Training (SLSST) program
description: The SLSST is a 21-week hands-on laboratory training curriculum implemented in 2012 in the Gynecologic Endoscopy and Endometriosis Fellowship Program, based on the Romeo Gladiator Rule seven-week activities. The article states it "consisted of a 21-week (4 hours per week) hands-on training at the experimental laboratory," with residents practicing a scheduled exercise a minimum of 4 hours weekly. It progresses through three phases: dominant hand on the lateral trocar (weeks 1–7), dominant hand on the central trocar (weeks 8–14), and non-dominant hand on the lateral trocar (weeks 15–21), repeating the same exercise sequence each phase. Core exercises include gladiator navigation, knot technique, needle and guidelines, staggered stitches, simple stitch with knot, vaginal apex suturing, and myomectomy sutures.
requirements: Residents practice the scheduled exercise for a minimum of 4 hours per week in an experimental laboratory
Training follows the Romeo Gladiator Rule seven-week activity sequence
Surgeries performed during the first 14 weeks (dominant-hand training period) were excluded from the post-training outcome group
constraints: Implemented and evaluated at a single Brazilian teaching hospital with 4 first-year and 2 second-year fellowship residents per year
target_learners: PGY-4 OB/GYN first-year fellowship residents in gynecologic endoscopy
examples: Surgeries in group I-3 were performed by PGY-4 residents after SLSST, supervised by a PGY-5 resident who had completed the same program the previous year
key_sources: Lobão Gonçalves Anna Luiza, Ayroza-Ribeiro Helizabet Abdala, Lima Raquel Ferreira, Yonamine Aline Estefane Eras, Ohara Fabio, Ayroza-Ribeiro Paulo Augusto Galvão. (2019). article_title: Associations between sleep deficit and academic achievement - triangulation across time and subject domains among students and teachers in TIMSS in Norway.
citation: Vik Frøydis N., Nilsen Trude, Øverby Nina C. (2022). Associations between sleep deficit and academic achievement - triangulation across time and subject domains among students and teachers in TIMSS in Norway. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-022-14161-1
title: Sleep and other health behaviors should be discussed within the education system, not only the private sphere
description: The article argues that sleep, as a health behavior, belongs on the education agenda: "health behaviors are important for academic achievements and should, therefore, be discussed in the education system". Because sleep deficits explained part of the decline in mathematics and science achievement, the authors call for discussion of sleep-duration recommendations and their dissemination across the educational and health systems, and for action beyond the private sphere, including from politicians.
requirements: The educational and health systems should discuss recommendations for sleep duration and how to disseminate such recommendations
constraints: Sleep is a factor in the private sphere, with parental responsibility playing a big part
The supporting TIMSS data are cross-sectional, so causality cannot be inferred
target_learners: Norwegian 9th-grade adolescents in lower secondary school
target_learning_goals: Maintaining and improving academic achievement in mathematics and science
examples: The study triangulated student-reported sleepiness, teacher-reported sleep deficits, and trend mediation analyses across two TIMSS cycles to argue that sleep deficits explain part of the achievement decline
key_sources: Vik Frøydis N., Nilsen Trude, Øverby Nina C. (2022). Associations between sleep deficit and academic achievement - triangulation across time and subject domains among students and teachers in TIMSS in Norway. BMC Public Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-022-14161-1

article_title: Game On-Complier Average Causal Effect Estimation Reveals Sleeper Effects on Academic Attainment in a Randomized Trial of the Good Behavior Game.
citation: Ashworth Emma, Panayiotou Margarita, Humphrey Neil, Hennessey Alexandra. (2020). Game On—Complier Average Causal Effect Estimation Reveals Sleeper Effects on Academic Attainment in a Randomized Trial of the Good Behavior Game. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-019-01074-6
title: Sleeper effects in universal school-based prevention: delayed emergence of effects contingent on implementation variability
description: A sleeper effect is "whereby enlarged positive effects are identified at later follow-up, compared to immediately post-intervention" (van Aar et al. 2017). This article extends the account by arguing, citing Greenberg and Abenavoli (2017), that "not all preventive effects are immediate as it takes time for changes in the intervention group population to consolidate", and adds "another layer of complexity, suggesting that the emergence of sleeper effects can be contingent upon implementation variability during the intervention period". The GBG's theorized mechanism is socializing children into the student role, increasing attention and on-task behavior, with disruptive behaviors reduced.
requirements: Multiple outcome measurement points over extended periods, since "when posttest-only studies conclude there are no impacts, such results are at best inconclusive" (Greenberg and Abenavoli 2017).
constraints: The mechanism linking compliance to later attainment is hypothesized, not yet formally tested: the authors state mediation via disruptive behavior "will be formally examined in a future paper".
examples: In the trial, no effect appeared at post-test in ITT or CACE models, yet a significant effect emerged among moderate compliers at 1-year follow-up.
key_sources: Ashworth Emma, Panayiotou Margarita, Humphrey Neil, Hennessey Alexandra. (2020). Game On—Complier Average Causal Effect Estimation Reveals Sleeper Effects on Academic Attainment in a Randomized Trial of the Good Behavior Game. Prevention Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-019-01074-6

article_title: Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing.
citation: Phillips, Andrew J. K.; Clerx, William M.; O'Brien, Conor S.; Sano, Akane; Barger, Laura K.; Picard, Rosalind W.; Lockley, Steven W.; Klerman, Elizabeth B.; Czeisler, Charles A. (2017). Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-03171-4
title: Sleep Regularity Index (SRI): a metric quantifying day-to-day probability of being in the same sleep/wake state 24 h apart
description: The Sleep Regularity Index is a novel metric introduced in this article to quantify sleep regularity. It "calculates the percentage probability of an individual being in the same state (asleep vs. awake) at any two time-points 24 h apart", scaled so a perfectly periodic sleeper scores 100 and a random sleeper scores 0. Unlike prior variability metrics, it "does not require designation of a main daily sleep episode", making it suitable for populations with naps and all-nighters such as college students. It was used to classify participants into Regular (top quintile) and Irregular (bottom quintile) groups at study midpoint.
requirements: Requires multi-day sleep/wake records (diaries or similar) to compute same-state probability across 24-h intervals; the article notes more data is needed to reliably estimate it for irregular sleepers.
constraints: The article notes no measure of sleep regularity can be perfectly estimated from a finite study interval, and SRI captures day-to-day differences in patterns rather than timing of a main sleep episode.
target_learners: populations with polyphasic or irregular sleep schedules
target_learning_goals: quantifying sleep regularity as a modifiable factor related to academic performance and circadian timing
examples: Used on 30 days of online sleep diaries from 61 undergraduates; midpoint classification into Regular (SRI 81-87) and Irregular (SRI 35-64) quintiles remained significantly different at 30 days (p < 10^-4).
key_sources: Phillips, Andrew J. K.; Clerx, William M.; O'Brien, Conor S.; Sano, Akane; Barger, Laura K.; Picard, Rosalind W.; Lockley, Steven W.; Klerman, Elizabeth B.; Czeisler, Charles A. (2017). Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-03171-4

article_title: Learning pathology using collaborative vs. individual annotation of whole slide images: a mixed methods trial.
citation: Sahota Michael, Leung Betty, Dowdell Stephanie, Velan Gary M. (2016). Learning pathology using collaborative vs. individual annotation of whole slide images: a mixed methods trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0831-x
title: Slice collaborative whole slide image annotation platform
description: Slice is a biomedical image repository and image viewer adopted by UNSW via the BEST Network, whose functionality "was enhanced to enable users to collaboratively annotate WSIs in real-time". Learners share annotations on a common image layer from any device and location, can view peers' annotations, and edit their own annotations in response, producing a group "consensus annotation". The study used Slice for both individual and collaborative annotation conditions in Pathology practical classes.
requirements: Web browser access to served whole slide images
Randomly self-allocated groups of 3–5 students for the collaborative condition
constraints: Students reported issues with the technology and interface limitations, such as instructions no longer being visible once annotation started and inability for all group members to edit layers simultaneously
target_learners: Biomedical and medical students learning histology and histopathology
target_learning_goals: Identification of microscopic histopathological features of disease processes
examples: Students in the trial annotated WSIs of tubular adenoma, colorectal carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue, invasive ductal carcinoma, diffuse alveolar damage, pulmonary carcinoid, endometrial adenocarcinoma and herpes oesophagitis
key_sources: Sahota Michael, Leung Betty, Dowdell Stephanie, Velan Gary M. (2016). Learning pathology using collaborative vs. individual annotation of whole slide images: a mixed methods trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0831-x
